national.title: U.S. reportedly floated trading Ukrainian land for NATO membership
national.summary: The Ukrainian president said he would put the question of the potential exchange its people, if certain guarantees are put in place.
national.body: U.S. negotiators asked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to consider giving up a part of his country exchange for NATO membership, the leader claimed.Zelenskyy told journalists on Friday he had been asked for the first time whether he would withdraw from the eastern region of Donbas in exchange for membership to the military alliance."The Americans raised a question: "What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?" This was the first time this had been raised," the Ukrainian president said.Zelenskyy said he was discussing a "security package" for Ukraine which included security guarantees from NATO and the European Union, an "adequate number of troops, weapons" as well as financial support. The Ukrainian president said if these measures are offered, he would ask Ukrainians whether to accept the potential exchange. He did not specify if he meant a referendum, but added "I have no right to make that decision on my own."Control over the Donbas region, much of which has been occupied by Russia since the start of the war, has been a recurring sticking point in negotiations to end the conflict. Russian President Vladimir Putin has previously demanded that Ukraine pull its forces out of the Donbas region as a precondition for a peace agreement.After staging elections dismissed by most of the world as a sham in occupied parts of the Donbas region, Putin declared in September 2022 that four regions of eastern Ukraine had also been annexed by Russia. None of the annexations have been recognized by the U.S. or the United Nations, and most countries consider them illegal landgrabs.Zelenskyy said he told U.S. negotiators Ukraine would need security guarantees modelled on NATO's Article 5 "as an asbolute minimum." That article sets out a key principle for the military alliance, whereby an attack on one of the member-states is considered an attack on all other members.The Ukrainian president added he was "not sure it would necessarily work," and said he needed more specific details on the potential membership.

national.title: UPS plane, passenger jet collide on Miami airport taxiway
national.summary: The collision comes as MIA continues to experience delays and cancellations​ following Friday's rare nationwide ground stop​ issued by the FAA.
national.body: A cargo plane and a commercial passenger jet collided at Miami International Airport Saturday night, officials said. A UPS Boeing 767 and a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 reportedly collided at the airport, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said."At approximately 9:15 p.m., an arriving aircraft and a departing aircraft made contact with each other at the intersection of two taxiways. There are no reported injuries and flights are being directed to other taxiways, so there is no impact to airport operations at this time," Greg Chin, communications director at MIA, said in a statement to CBS News Miami.Chin said two patients were treated on the scene by Miami-Dade Fire Rescue for minor injuries and did not require medical transport. UPS Flight 358 was scheduled to fly from Miami to Bogotá, Colombia, and Copa Airlines Flight 427 was arriving from Panama City, Panama. Copa Airlines is headquartered in Panama City. The collision comes as MIA continues to experience delays and cancellations following Friday's rare nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration.Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned Friday night that flight operations would be slow to return to normal as airlines worked to reposition aircraft and crews.FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Saturday that the U.S. air travel schedule should be back to normal by the end of Sunday.Federal officials said the outage was linked to problems with aging air traffic control technology, including switches and routers that became overloaded with data, creating inconsistencies in radar and communications systems.

national.title: Three men sentenced to death in Jordan over fatal church mass shooting
national.summary: The attack on funeral at a Greek Orthodox church killed nine and injured 34 others last month.
national.body:
A Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out a fatal mass shooting on a church last month.

The attack on 23 October killed nine people and injured 34 others who had been attending a Christian funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate.

Jordan's Armed Forces said in a statement on Sunday that the men had been convicted of committing "terrorist acts", as well as possessing weapons, "promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation" and "conspiracy to commit terrorist acts".

The three men - two Jordanian brothers and their brother-in-law - fled the scene of the attack and were arrested three days later. They have not been publicly identified.

Karak is home to a sizeable Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom.

CCTV footage from the day of the attack showed three men holding guns approaching and firing on St George's church in the village of Hmoud.

A second video showed dead and wounded people lying on the ground amid chaotic scenes at the church.

It is still unclear why the attackers chose to target that specific church.

national.title: A new generation of disability rights activists carry on Judy Heumann's legacy
national.summary: The film Being Heumann tells the lesser-known story of the mother of the disability rights movement. A new generation of activists share how they "carry the torch" today.
national.body:
Andrew Pilkington, Siena Rafter, Charlie Rush-Reese, Dylan O'Brien, Roberta Colindrez, Ruth Madeley and Madeline Delp in Being Heumann , premiering November 13, 2026 on Apple TV. Apple TV hide caption

Judy Heumann is known as the mother of the disability rights movement — yet she is lesser known than many of the other civil rights activists of her time. Now, a new film seeks to change that.

Being Heumann , the latest movie from Oscar-winning director Sian Heder , tells the story of the young woman from Brooklyn who led the movement to win the first civil rights protections in the country for people with disabilities.

Before the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) was passed in 1990, there was Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 . It was a single sentence, written into the law, promising people with disabilities the right to fair employment and access to public life without facing discrimination.

But for years, there were no rules or regulations making the federal government actually enforce those protections.

Until the spring of 1977, when a band of activists with disabilities decided to do something about it. Led by Heumann and Kitty Cone, activists took over the former Department of Health, Education and Welfare building in San Francisco for nearly a month — widely considered the longest sit-in of a federal building in U.S. history.

People across disability groups — from wheelchair users to people with intellectual and health-related disabilities — camped out, demanding, and eventually winning the passage of rules that made Section 504 enforceable. The protests paved the way for federally funded institutions like schools, libraries, city buildings and other entities to be made accessible for disabled people.

"Judy always said, 'disability only becomes a tragedy for me when society fails to provide the things we need to lead our lives' — job opportunities or barrier-free buildings, for example," says former NPR correspondent Joe Shapiro, who covered disability and was a friend of Heumann's until she died in 2023.

national.title: Pope Leo speaks of community 'suffering' on visit to remote Andes town
national.summary: Santa Cruz de Succhabamba is part of the Diocese of Chiclayo, where the Pope served as bishop from 2015 to 2023.
national.body:
Pope Leo XIV has spoken about the "suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future", which he said had left communities under threat, during a visit to an isolated Andean village in his former diocese.

About 6,000 people live in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, located in a remote part of the Andes mountains of northern Peru, but the Pope's visit still drew a crowd of about 20,000, according to the Vatican.

At an outdoor Mass, the Pope spoke of "declining birth rates that are emptying villages" and the unequal distribution of the land's resources.

More than 40% of the population in the Cajamarca region, where the town is located, live in poverty - the highest figure in Peru, according to official data.

Cajamarca has lost the highest number of people to internal migration, with 729,000 people born there now living elsewhere in Peru.

In his sermon, the Pope thanked those who had made the journey to see him and emphasised the importance of never losing heart, despite life's difficulties.

The pontiff's Latin America tour comes roughly a month after he underwent surgery to remove part of his right lung after a cancerous lump was found during routine checks.

At the start of his trip, he said the care he had received made him think of those who "lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis" or receive treatment for health conditions.

national.title: Fifth Canadian soldier dies from injuries caused by large fire at military base
national.summary: Pte William Douglas Dal Bianco died from his injuries on Friday, a month after a fire that tore through CFB Wainwright.
national.body:
A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries he suffered when a grass fire swept through a military training area last month.

Four people were killed initially and dozens were injured when the fire, which ignited during a live fire training exercise, spread rapidly through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright carried by strong winds on 17 October.

Pte William Douglas Dal Bianco, who had been receiving medical care in Ontario, died on Friday, the Canadian Armed Forces said in a statement.

Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote on X: "Canadians are holding Private Dal Bianco's loved ones, and all those still grieving in the wake of this terrible tragedy, in our hearts."

The Canadian Armed Forces said that 24 military personnel were still in hospital receiving treatment, while 14 had been released as of Saturday. Thirty-eight military personnel had been injured in total.

Members of 1 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group had been conducting live-fire training at the base, in the province of Alberta, when the fire broke out.

Military officials said at the time that the fire spread across a kilometre in a matter of seconds, taking many of those on the base by surprise.

Firefighters battled the blaze through the night, while nearby hospitals became inundated by injured personnel and staff.

national.title: Israel kills Hamas commander in strike on Gaza camp, officials say
national.summary: Both Hamas and IDF officials confirm the death of Samir Abu Younis, commander of the Rafah Brigade.
national.body:
A senior Hamas figure who helped plan and oversee the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel has been killed in an Israeli airstrike, officials in Israel and Gaza have said.

Samir Abu Younis, the newly appointed commander of the Rafah Brigade, was killed on Saturday in Al-Mawasi in the southern Gaza Strip, according to Hamas's Al-Qassam Brigades military wing.

A local Hamas official confirmed Younis's death. The Israeli military said it had targeted him and that prior to the strike "steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians".

Eyewitnesses in Gaza said four missiles struck a tent in the Al-Waha camp, which shelters hundreds of displaced people in Al-Mawasi, causing a fire to break out.

A medical source at Nasser Hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis said three injured people had arrived there, as well as a dead body.

The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) and Israel's security agency, the ISA, confirmed in a statement on Telegram that it had "eliminated" Younis.

Describing him as a "central figure among Hamas's senior figures", it said he had "acted with the aim of trying to restore the strength of the brigade and the Hamas terrorist organisation".

It added: "Younis directed the brigade's terrorists to advance and carry out terror attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF troops."

national.title: Copper wire upgrade behind US flight suspension, transport secretary says
national.summary: The US government is trying to find out whether the chaos was caused by "incompetence" or faulty equipment.
national.body:
A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations and prompted travel chaos was caused by a technical issue following a copper wire upgrade, the transport secretary has said.

Sean Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem that led to air traffic controllers suspending take-offs for four hours on Friday had been caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades or faulty equipment.

Though the ground stop was lifted on Friday evening, it had a knock-on effect on air travel on Saturday as airlines attempted to clear a backlog of flights.

Officials including Duffy had previously attributed the issue to outdated equipment.

Maintenance on US air traffic control systems was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre-optic cable by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider, Duffy said.

The US had "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he said, adding: "It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued."

The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes, prompting the shutdown on safety grounds.

The government was now trying to understand whether the root cause was the wire replacement or a fault with the router.

national.body: Tucked in off the road to Mount Hood, the Hoodland Plaza Shopping Center serves as a gathering place for the people of Welches, Oregon, where they sometimes get things that money just can't buy.Sarah Caswell: It's kind of a — a community hub … if someone needed to vent or talk or … need help, that's where they'd go.The plaza is home to Sarah Caswell's pizza shop and the neighboring Hoodland Bazaar – the whimsical gift shop where her friend Phoenix Lane worked. Sarah Caswell: November 22, 2024, we showed up to work … and she hadn't showed up. Phoenix was supposed to open the store at 11 a.m. that Friday.Sarah Caswell: She hadn't put the signs out yet. And I was like, that's crazy … she would never not show up.The search for Susan "Phoenix" LanePhoenix's boss tried texting her, but she didn't respond. national.title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from moving ahead on Washington public golf course redevelopment
national.summary: A federal judge on Saturday ordered a two-week delay to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House.
national.body:
Temporary fencing is seen at East Potomac Park, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. Tom Brenner/AP hide caption

WASHINGTON — A federal judge on Saturday ordered a two-week delay to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House, blocking for now President Donald Trump's push to redevelop the site along the Potomac River into a championship-level venue.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. Trump had announced work would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.

The plaintiffs argue that Trump's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the Republican president denies. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would "irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."

The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the decision. Trump said on Oct. 26 that "We are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons." He added that the goal was to renovate and rebuild "a World Championship Public Facility."

Reyes in her ruling Saturday noted that Trump's posts presented a problem for the government. "They indicate that the Washington National Plan is final and that NPS will close the Park to implement it," she wrote. "Both points favor granting Plaintiffs' motion for another temporary restraining order."

Reyes said her order "ENJOINS the government from closing East Potomac Park and the East Potomac Golf Course during the daily hours in which they were open as of November 14, 2026. It does not order the Government to undertake any active management of either. Further, for the avoidance of any doubt, the Government remains free, as it has since the onset of this litigation, to conduct repairs on any part of the Park and Course with any notice required by the existing Preliminary Injunction."

The judge said the order is in effect "through November 28, 2026, or further order from the Court, whichever comes first."

national.title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from closing Washington DC golf course for renovation
national.summary: It is the latest development in a months-long challenge to the US president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links.
national.body:
A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of an historic golf course and park in Washington DC.

US District Judge Ana Reyes has been overseeing a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, which he said would be closed from 15 November for extensive renovations.

Reyes has said Donald Trump cannot close the park nor its golf course, but added that his administration was not required to actively manage either.

Trump, an avid golfer, has said his plans to upgrade the 106-year-old course will create "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World". The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

Declaring the current course "Trash Island", he announced in October that it would be renovated over 15 months to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments" - despite the ongoing litigation.

Reyes said in a 30-page decision issued on Saturday that the Trump administration's justifications for the proposed course closures were pretextual and that the government had violated at least two federal laws "to meet an arbitrary deadline".

"The government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely," Reyes wrote.

She said the closure "runs counter to the public interest in utilising national parkland", adding that the government had not "plausibly identified any harm it would suffer from a temporary restraining order that preserves the status quo pending further proceedings".

national.title: FAA ground stop disrupts college football
national.summary: Some college football games were delayed a few hours on Saturday or postponed to Sunday. And in Oklahoma at least, there will be perks for fans to make up for the inconvenience, including cheap beers.
national.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration's ground stop on Friday has led not only to travel headaches, but also schedule changes and delays in college sports.

Many college football teams were in airports Friday on their way to upcoming games when the nationwide ground stop was issued and thousands of flights were canceled. The FAA on Saturday said airports were returning to normal operations, but that delays and cancellations would continue through the day.

Transportation FAA blames Friday's ground stop on 'equipment issue' during telecoms network upgrade Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy acknowledged the ground stop's impact on college football. Several games on Saturday were delayed for hours.

"If you look at the cost of what happened yesterday, we're talking if you like football — I know we've had some disruptions to the college football schedule. Some games are being moved," Duffy said during a news conference Saturday. "That's not the most important thing, but we do want to move teams around the country so we can have playoffs happen."

Utah, ranked No. 2 in the College Football Playoff Rankings , will kick off against Arizona in Tucson at 8:30 p.m. local time — a three-hour delay. The Auburn vs. Mississippi State game was pushed back more than four hours to start at 3:15 p.m. local time in Mississippi because of the ground stop. The Florida Atlantic Owls were also unable to fly to Oklahoma on Friday ahead of their game against the Tulsa Golden Hurricane. Saturday's game, which was supposed to begin at 2:30 p.m. local time, was moved to 6:15 p.m. local time.

While other college teams were able to arrive at their destinations and proceed with games on Saturday, the University of Mississippi did not.

Ole Miss, ranked No. 19, was not able to fly to Oklahoma as planned on Friday for its matchup with the University of Oklahoma Sooners. The game between the two teams, which was scheduled to occur Saturday, will now take place on Sunday at 1 p.m. ET, according to the Southeastern Conference . The game will compete with several NFL games that will be televised at the same time. NFL teams were largely unaffected by the ground stop.

In order to help alleviate fans' frustration, the Sooners on Saturday announced "fan appreciation" promotions for the rescheduled game. Oklahoma students can go to the game for free with their student ID and there will be reduced prices on concession items such as $2 for popcorn or a 16-ounce beer.

national.title: Judo champion shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy
national.summary: Teddy Riner is one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, and one in five voters say they could support him.
national.body:
Apart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection between politics and the world of top-level judo.

That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race.

The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.

But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances.

Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business.

More than 28 million people have watched his election broadcast on Instagram and X, shot with proper presidential decorum against a backdrop of books and a French flag. Some 22% told an Ifop poll within 24 hours they "could" vote for him.

Actors and television personalities have become presidents in other countries. The ex-leader of Liberia – George Weah – was formerly a professional footballer.

"Anyone who thinks that being out of the political in-crowd disqualifies Riner from running for the Élysée would be very wrong," says Guillaume Tabard of Le Figaro.

national.title: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
national.summary: Fear and misinformation surrounds the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo - Dr Kamwanga's mother was not immune.
national.body:
When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.

They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there.

"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.

But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.

This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.

Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.

Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.

After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience.

national.title: Florida city cancels St. Patrick's Day parade, citing new anti-DEI law
national.summary: A new Florida law that prohibits taxpayer dollars from going toward diversity initiatives has prompted Delray Beach to cancel its St. Patrick's Day parade after a nearly 60-year run.
national.body:
One of the first casualties of a new Florida law that prohibits taxpayer dollars from going toward diversity initiatives is a St. Patrick's Day parade in a beach town that has been celebrating its Irish American community for nearly 60 years.

Education Amid Trump's assaults on DEI, how one university is elevating Black students The city of Delray Beach announced this week that it was canceling its popular St. Patrick's Day festivities in compliance with a new law that takes effect on Jan. 1. The city will also withdraw its sponsorship of LGBTQ Pride celebrations in June, officials said.

The law, backed by Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is part of the state's ongoing crackdown on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives that the governor has called discriminatory and said have "no place" in public institutions.

The city lawyer for Delray Beach, a community in southeast Florida with picturesque beaches and a historic downtown, told the mayor that any government-sponsored celebrations of culture, ethnicity or heritage that are not a national holiday (for example: Independence Day) could run afoul of the new anti-DEI law. So, Mayor Tom Carney said, he made the difficult decision to cancel one of the city's biggest events of the year.

The State of the First Amendment 'What did I say in class today?': Teachers feel watched under Trump's anti-DEI push In past years, the parade, an annual event since 1970, wound its way through the downtown core of Delray Beach with spectators lined up several-people deep along the route. Local businesses and organizations sponsored floats and giveaways. School bands played as they marched through the streets. Participants included members of the Ancient Order of Hibernians, the largest and oldest Irish Catholic organization in the country.

"I've said it's engrained in the DNA of Delray and I do mean that. It's one of our signature events," Carney, a Republican, told NPR.

The mayor said he's hopeful that the city can find a path forward — and a way to preserve the event.

If a private sponsor were to volunteer to take over the St. Patrick's Day parade, or the June Pride celebrations, Carney said, the city would gladly hand over the reins and support the continuation of these festivities.

national.summary: At least three people were killed and two others were severely injured when an SUV crashed into a food stand near a Metro bus stop in North Hollywood.
national.body: Police say three people are dead after an SUV crashed into a food stand near a North Hollywood bus stop in Los Angeles on Tuesday night. The collision occurred at around 5:55 p.m. local time near the Metro station at the corner of Lankershim and Chandler boulevards, according to the LA Police Department. Firefighters said three people were pronounced dead at the scene, while three others were taken to a nearby hospital, two of whom were in critical condition at the time. As of 11 p.m., one of the victims remained in stable condition, while the other was still critical.On Wednesday, the LA County Medical Examiner identified two of the victims as 57-year-old Teodora Villalobos and 73-year-old Maria Peck. The third victim was identified as 39-year-old Francesca Krystine Esker on Friday.Witnesses told CBS LA the three women were street vendors in the area, and one had worked there for more than 15 years.The critically injured individuals are also women between 50 and 55 years old.Crews extricated one person, the driver, from the wreckage, according to LAFD."I'm heartbroken for the families of everyone impacted," Mayor Karen Bass wrote in a statement on X. "We will continue to provide updates as more information becomes available."LAPD officers said the driver of the white SUV was in serious condition and was determined to be under the influence of drugs or alcohol at the time of the crash. Police identified him as Ihor Demianenko, a 61-year-old Valley Village resident. He was arrested on suspicion of three counts of murder.Demianenko is currently being held on more than $6 million bail.The circumstances surrounding the collision remain under investigation, but LAPD Major Collision Investigation Team and Valley Traffic Division detectives said that Demianenko was attempting to avoid another car that was driving "legally and safely" before the crash. Police said they would continue looking for security camera footage from the Metro bus station and businesses in the surrounding area as their probe continued."It'll be a prolonged but a very deliberate investigation to determine what happened here," LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell said. "Planes are pushing back, taxiing, and taking off, and it is safe to fly," Duffy said earlier in a social media post on Saturday. He's scheduled to appear on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday."You will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most."More than 5,000 flights were canceled Saturday, according to flight tracking website FlightAware, while around 5,300 others were delayed. national.title: 5th Canadian soldier dies weeks after fire on military base
national.summary: Pvt. William Douglas Dal Bianco died Friday at a hospital in Ontario, where he had been receiving treatment since the Oct. 17 fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, the military said.
national.body: A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries suffered when a wind-driven grass fire swept through troops during a military training exercise last month, the Canadian Armed Forces said Saturday.Pvt. William Douglas Dal Bianco died Friday at a hospital in Ontario, where he had been receiving treatment since the Oct. 17 fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, the military said.About 84 soldiers from the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, were conducting attack training when winds pushed flames from a grass fire toward the troops at the base southeast of Edmonton. It occurred on a grenade launcher range, officials said last month.The military said Saturday that 24 soldiers remain hospitalized."Private Dal Bianco and his fellow soldiers were training to defend Canada," Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a social media post. "With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours. That is service."The other soldiers killed were Pvt. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Saskatchewan; Pvt. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, British Columbia; Pvt. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, British Columbia; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.Military police are investigating the fire, while a separate military board of inquiry will examine the circumstances of the tragedy and recommend measures to prevent similar incidents.Maj. Gen. Wade Rutland said that military officials knew about the fire for hours but believed it was contained and allowed training to continue before winds suddenly shifted.Carney has called the fire one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada's military on Canadian soil. "We will get the answers to what caused this terrible tragedy, as expeditiously and transparently as necessary," Carney told reporters last month.

national.title: How telecoms upgrade work sparked US flight chaos
national.summary: US officials say the disruption was caused by old equipment overloading and not a cyber-attack.
national.body:
An upgrade to a decades-old telecoms network in the US caused the longest nationwide grounding of flights since the 11 September 2001 attacks.

Friday's stoppage occurred when part of a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate was switched to fibre from copper wiring so old it has been discontinued, said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday.

US planes were grounded for more than four hours, affecting thousands of flights and passengers.

Earlier Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyber-attack and that everybody was safe.

On Friday afternoon, a government contractor called L3Harris was continuing work on upgrading an aviation telecoms network.

As it swapped out copper lines for fibre at a remote location in the US, L3Harris installed a router - a piece of equipment which basically directs traffic across the network.

According to Duffy, that router started flooding others in the air traffic control system, sending 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds.

As a result, 17 out of 22 air route traffic control centres in the US experienced "instability" on voice and ground communications, said Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

national.title: SpaceX pulls off first Starship recovery from orbit in spectacular fashion
national.summary: It was the first recovery of a Starship from orbit, a major milestone for a rocket SpaceX founder Elon Musk says will dramatically lower launch costs.
national.body: After a 22-hour stay in space, a SpaceX Starship rocket plunged back to Earth Saturday, enduring the blazing heat of reentry while homing in on its Texas Gulf Coast launch site, flipping vertical at the last moment and settling into the grasp of two huge mechanical arms on its launch gantry.Throngs of SpaceX employees gathered nearby cheered and applauded as the rocket restarted three of its six methane-fueled Raptor engines to flip upright, rapidly slowing to a near hover as the robot arms moved in for a mechanical embrace, catching the rocket a moment before engine shutdown."This is so incredible to see!" said SpaceX commentator Jessie Anderson. "One of the most incredible and historic engineering feats of all time has just happened right in front of our eyes. Congratulations to our teammates at SpaceX, and to everyone who supported the Starship program."It was the first such recovery of a Starship from orbit — previous test flights ended with planned ocean splashdowns — marking a major milestone in SpaceX's drive to develop the first fully reusable orbit-class rocket, a vehicle company founder Elon Musk says will dramatically lower the cost of launching payloads to Earth orbit, the moon and, eventually, Mars.The Starship was launched atop a Super Heavy booster Friday using the same pad at SpaceX's Starbase facility on the Texas coast. Standing 407 feet tall, the two-stage rocket is the most powerful launcher ever built, generating some 16 million pounds of thrust at liftoff from 33 first-stage Raptor engines.After propelling the Starship upper stage out of the lower atmosphere, the Super Heavy first stage attempted its own return to the launch site for capture by the gantry's mechanical arms.Going into the giant rocket's 15th test flight, SpaceX had successfully recovered the first-stage boosters used in three previous launches. But the Super Heavy launched Friday was diverted to an offshore splashdown because of a guidance problem. The vehicle ran out of fuel and exploded moments before hitting the water.While a disappointment to the SpaceX team, Musk said in a posting on the social media platform X the problem was a "slight underperformance of engines," adding that "these early ships and boosters are already outdated by improved designs in production or on the test stand.""This booster loss does not change our timeline to reach high volume, fully reusab

national.title: Passengers rescued after tanker hit river cruise in New Orleans
national.summary: A tanker struck a river cruise ship on the Mississippi River near the Port of New Orleans Friday, partially submerging the passenger boat.
national.body: A major rescue operation took place Friday after a tanker struck a river cruise ship on the Mississippi River near the Port of New Orleans, leaving the American Heritage passenger boat on its side and largely submerged in the water. Everyone aboard both vessels has been accounted for, officials said, and there were no fatalities reported.The much larger tanker, identified as the Atlantic Asphalt, crashed into the paddlewheel cruise boat while it was docked at about 12:30 p.m. local time, the Port of New Orleans said. The American Heritage had docked about two hours earlier for passengers to disembark. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said in a news briefing late Friday afternoon that 32 passengers from the cruise ship were taken to area hospitals for treatment, but none with critical injuries. No one aboard the tanker was hurt, Moreno said. New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said two of her officers were also hospitalized during the rescue operation, but were in good condition.Eight people remained hospitalized Saturday afternoon, with two in serious condition, Moreno said at a news conference.There were 191 passengers and crew members aboard the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the mayor.Moreno said the tanker "lost control" and crashed into the cruise ship. As passengers were disembarking from the cruise ship, it "began to sink, and then eventually toppled over and flipped," sending people into the water, the mayor said.Some people were seen in the water in life jackets or standing near the railing as the other side of the ship listed farther into the water. Moreno said at a news conference Saturday that rescuers pulled approximately 100 people from the water. Nearby boats had reported rescuing more than a dozen people from the water. Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others, while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and currently controls most of the industrial Donbas region. Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory.

national.title: Why a problem on the ground can affect flights thousands of miles away among other issues
national.summary: Michael McCormick, a former airspace manager with the Federal Aviation Administration, said it could take days for airlines — many of which had to divert flights — to resume normal operations after officials lifted the grounding order.
national.body:
Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Becky Bohrer, Associated Press

Anne D'Innocenzio, Associated Press Anne D'Innocenzio, Associated Press

Regional U.S. air traffic control centers communicate using a complex network that's "one of the largest telecommunications systems in the country," and disruptions like those seen on Friday with an hourslong, nationwide grounding of flights can reverberate widely, according to an aviation expert.

Michael McCormick, a former airspace manager with the Federal Aviation Administration, said it could take days for airlines — many of which had to divert flights — to resume normal operations after officials lifted the grounding order. The order was lifted late Friday.

Here's a look at what happened, how regional air traffic control centers work, how controllers communicate with pilots and why a problem on the ground can affect flights thousands of miles away among other issues:

The nation's air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused "intermittent" communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours on Friday, Trump administration officials said Saturday in a press briefing.

A contractor had been working on replacing a section of the system's old and discontinued copper wire with new fiber wire in a remote location on Friday afternoon, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said Saturday. That kind of work has been happening across the country and across industries for decades, he said.

"Specifically, we had over 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds," Duffy said. "And what that did was gave us issues with our communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar feeds. And when we see that, your safety is paramount, we shut down the airspace."

national.title: New Orleans port files $1m lawsuit over 'miracle on the Mississippi' tanker collision
national.summary: The lawsuit filed by New Orleans officials also requests that the tanker involved in the collision with the cruise ship be seized and sold to pay for damages.
national.body:
The Port of New Orleans is suing the owners and managers of a tanker that crashed into a cruise ship docked there on Friday.

The port is claiming the tanker is at fault for the collision that saw more than 100 passengers being rescued from the Mississippi River and caused more than $1m (£756,000) in damage, according to court documents.

The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one was unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi".

The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Capt Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering."

The paddlewheel cruise ship, American Heritage, was left on its side and partially submerged in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel Atlantic Asphalt on Friday afternoon.

The court documents added that the port terminal had been "significantly damaged" in the incident.

The tanker, the M/V Atlantic Asphalt, its owner Nave Shipping SA and its management company Thome Ship Management Pte Ltd are all named in the lawsuit filed in federal court on Friday in the Eastern District of Louisiana.

Officials are still investigating the full extent of the damage from the crash, as well as the cause, but the lawsuit says the port is looking for money to cover clean-up, inspections, repairs and other expenses.

national.title: US has lost measles elimination status, global health authorities say
national.summary: The U.S. has lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, according to researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations at the Pan American Health Organization.
national.body:
Anna Fajardo, a public health nurse, offers vaccines at a school registration event in southwestern Utah. Amy Maxmen/KFF Health News hide caption

The U.S. has lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health triumph secured a quarter century ago.

Researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations on the country's status told KFF Health News that the Pan American Health Organization reached the conclusion this week: Measles has reestablished regular transmission in the country.

In public health parlance, measles elimination depends on a country's sporadic outbreaks ending within a year. That's no longer happening in the United States.

"It's a very sad moment," said Anne Schuchat, an epidemiologist and a former deputy director at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention who was not involved in PAHO's decision.

"Measles causes so much unnecessary suffering, everything from a high fever and missed work and school to long-term complications like progressive degenerative nerve disease and death," Schuchat said.

Measles outbreaks are entirely preventable: Two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine prevent about 97% of infections, so when almost everyone in a community is fully vaccinated, the virus can't spread.

In the past two years, over 830 people have been hospitalized with measles in the U.S. More than 8,000 people have been sickened in outbreaks that have cost roughly $125 million in medical care, public health response, and productivity losses, Johns Hopkins University researchers estimate .

national.title: SpaceX successfully catches top of huge Starship rocket for first time
national.summary: The rocket stage was caught mid air using huge mechanical arms nicknamed "chopsticks".
national.body:
SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket for the first time, after a flight lasting 22-and-a-half hours.

The rocket returned to Earth and hovered near its launch tower, whose mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - then secured it.

The company had hoped to catch the bottom part of the rocket as well, but this was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday.

SpaceX needs to reliably recover both parts of Starship so that it can fly repeatedly and drastically reduce costs.

There were loud cheers from SpaceX staff who were watching the flight as the rocket returned to the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas.

This is the 15th test of Starship and the first that hoped to fully recover both parts of the rocket. SpaceX wants to make the top and bottom sections of Starship fully reusable.

The 124m-tall (407ft) rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 16:47 local time (19:47 GMT) on Friday.

The plan was to grab the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six-and-a-half-minutes later when it returned.

national.title: SpaceX's Starship returns from orbit and is captured by launch pad arms in a dramatic first
national.summary: It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday's liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch.
national.body:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — SpaceX's Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.

It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday's liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch, still the goal for accelerating moon and Mars travel.

Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad.

The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster's messy miss. Cameras panned the spacecraft up and down as it hung high above the ground, supported by the arms of the launch tower.

"Can you believe it?" SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted, dragging out each word. "Look at her! Baby, she's back!"

Soon afterward, Musk congratulated his "incredible team." SpaceX officials said Saturday's catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, crucial for rapid and low-cost recycling. Although Friday's booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.

NASA welcomed Saturday's news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk's ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.

"It was almost magic," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X. "Making more believers by the day ... one step closer to (emojis of the moon and the U.S. flag)."

national.summary: Trump's tonal shifts have only added to the uncertainty about what comes next in a war in which America's allies were not consulted before it was started but nonetheless struggle to deal with its economic ramifications.
national.body:
Aamer Madhani, Associated Press Aamer Madhani, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump has had a lot to say about his thinking on the way ahead in the Iran war since Republicans were trounced in last week's midterm elections.

In exchanges with reporters, broadcast interviews and social media posts since Election Day, he's somehow managed to back away from carrying out additional strikes while also backing away from the prospect of additional talks with the Islamic Republic's negotiators on ending the 8-month-old conflict.

The president acknowledged on the day after the midterms that the war and the global economic tumult it's caused were partly to blame for Republicans' electoral losses, while maintaining it was the right thing to do.

Then, at the start of this week, he huddled with Qatar's prime minister at the White House and afterward told reporters that he believed it was highly unlikely he'd need to order new major strikes on Iran, declaring that the war "militarily is effectively over."

But by Thursday, he was again raising questions about whether he needed to rush to find an endgame. He declared that the U.S. no longer needs a deal with Tehran and brusquely directed Vice President JD Vance — who served as his chief negotiator in earlier peace talks with Iran — to shift his attention to the administration's domestic anti-fraud campaign targeting Democrat-controlled cities and states.

All the while, Trump warned Iran that the U.S. military is "locked and loaded" and keeping an eye on Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran's nuclear program, for signs of activity.

"If something does not work out, I would not hesitate" to act, Trump told conservative broadcaster Hugh Hewitt on Thursday.

national.title: The U.S. flu season is off to a very early start. It's hitting the South and West now
national.summary: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Friday posted its latest update, reporting that seven states were reporting high flu activity last week, up from two states the week before.
national.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — The U.S. flu season is off to a very early start, and it's quickly intensifying.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Friday posted its latest update, reporting that seven states were reporting high flu activity last week, up from two states the week before.

The CDC also said that more than 3% of doctors' office visits last week were for flu-like illness, signaling that flu season is really underway.

Flu season "is taking off and it's taking off in a direction that's only likely to increase in the next month or two," said Dr. Fred Lopez, an infectious diseases specialist at the LSU Health Sciences Center in New Orleans.

"If you haven't been vaccinated, you should get vaccinated now," he added.

The early-season flu activity is higher than what's usually seen at this point of the year, though it's not clear that will mean this season will be worse than others, according to CDC's update.

But not a good sign: The flu hospitalization rate in mid-October was the highest seen that early in an autumn in more than 15 years, noted Dr. Anna Durbin of Johns Hopkins University, during a recent media briefing.

The CDC estimates that at least 2.6 million illnesses, 36,000 hospitalizations, and 2,100 deaths so far this season are tied to flu infections.

national.title: Bomb found near ethanol plant in central Illinois forces evacuations
national.summary: The bomb was discovered Friday afternoon at the BioUrja Renewables plant in Peoria. Officials say the bomb has been "rendered safe," but called it a "credible threat." The FBI is investigating.
national.body:
A bomb was found near an ethanol plant in central Illinois, sparking evacuations of those who live near the industrial site as law enforcement officials investigate, authorities said Saturday.

The bomb was found Friday afternoon at the BioUrja Renewables facility in Peoria. While officials say the device has since been "rendered safe," as of Saturday morning, all residents within a 1-mile radius remained under an evacuation notice as officials continued to scour the facility for any other bombs and evidence.

Meanwhile, shelters have been set up for those displaced by the threat, authorities said.

"This is a credible threat," Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon told reporters just after midnight Saturday. "We need to take the blast radius seriously."

FBI Special Agent Ryan Pressley said his agency was investigating, but declined to provide further details.

"We will work tirelessly to identify the individual responsible and bring them to justice," he said.

No arrests have been made at this time and no injuries have been reported.

Peoria Mayor Rita Ali told WMBD-TV on Friday that BioUrja is "a plant that has ethanol and highly combustible types of chemicals, and so that's what alarms us."

local.title: Senator seeks to overturn Freedom Tax Credit opt-in
local.summary: State Democrats’ newly restored veto-proof supermajority may get a test next year over New York’s opt-in to President Donald Trump’s Education Freedom Tax Credit program. Gov. Kathy Hochul opted into the program in October, joining several other states. Not all Democrats in the state Legislature are
local.body:
State Democrats' newly restored veto-proof supermajority may get a test next year over New York's opt-in to President Donald Trump's Education Freedom Tax Credit program.

Gov. Kathy Hochul opted into the program in October, joining several other states. Not all Democrats in the state Legislature are happy with the move, however, including Sen. John Liu, D-Bayside. Liu recently introduced S.10734, which would amend the state Education Law to designate the state Board of Regents as the sole entity responsible for determining whether New York state will participate in the program as well as requiring the Board of Regents to determine and submit the state’s list of qualified scholarship granting organizations to the federal government.

If passed, Liu's legislation would give the Board of Regents the authority on an annual basis to decide whether New York would participate in the voucher program beginning with the 2028 tax year. Liu had opposed the program before Hochul opted New York into the program.

"However the Trump administration may spin it, this tax credit is a federal voucher program, an idea long debated and rejected in the state of New York because it inevitably diverts resources away from public schools. Though public schools may receive some of the donations eligible to be refunded as tax credits, the clear intent is to subsidize private schools, with the public education funding already cut by the administration. New York should not buy into this terrible policy, advanced by a now lame-duck administration, which has some likelihood of being reversed in the near future," Liu said. "Regardless of what the political arguments may be, this program is a matter of education policy best decided by the state Board of Regents which for over 200 years has set policy for all schools in New York State in a manner largely shielded from the prevailing politics of the times. This legislation appropriately places this matter in the hands of the Board of Regents."

Nearly all schoolchildren in at least 30 states can apply for a new federal scholarship next year to help pay for private school, homeschooling and other educational expenses, according to regulations proposed Thursday by the Trump administration.

The first national school choice scholarship program, the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit, will launch Jan. 1, establishing a taxpayer-funded incentive for families to choose private or homeschooling in participating states. Taxpayers who donate to an organization passing out the scholarships will receive a federal tax credit, a perk expected to further fuel the conservative school choice movement. Taxpayers will have the chance to donate to a scholarship program in a participating state, even if they do not live there, starting Jan. 1. Individuals can donate up to $1,700 and receive a federal tax credit for the same amount in exchange. Federal officials propose a couple filing jointly could give as much as double that amount. Scholarship organizations in each state would decide how much to grant to each child who applies, depending on available funds and student need. Children could qualify if they are in elementary through high school and their families earn up to three times the area's median income. For a family of four in Houston, for example, that equates to more than $300,000.

local.title: Centaur Stride needs succession plan to keep riding
local.summary: They say the only two certainties in life are death and taxes. The difference is that we know exactly when our taxes are due. The timing of the other is never quite so certain. Perhaps the best we can do is make the most of the time we have: play the cards we are dealt, […]
local.body:
They say the only two certainties in life are death and taxes. The difference is that we know exactly when our taxes are due. The timing of the other is never quite so certain.

Perhaps the best we can do is make the most of the time we have: play the cards we are dealt, make changes where we can, and leave things a little better than we found them.

That has been my motivation for the past 36 years in building Centaur Stride.

What began as a 4-H program in our backyard grew into a three-year journey of planning, building and overcoming obstacles before finally finding its home between Westfield and Sherman. After nearly a year of searching, we found the only property we could afford. We believed in the philosophy, "Build it and they will come." We were convinced that therapeutic horseback riding could make a meaningful difference in people’s lives, and we were determined to make it happen.

Friends rallied to help, challenges were overcome, and there was no turning back. When you care for live animals, the work doesn’t stop simply because people don’t show up. The horses still need feeding, care and attention. The bills still need paying. Success meant showing up every day, never giving up and finding a way to keep going.

For many years, the daily demands left little time to think about the future. Strategic planning, sustainability and long-term projections seemed distant luxuries when there was so much to accomplish just to get through another day.

Grants are not guaranteed. First, an organization must prove its worth. Then it must demonstrate a credible plan for sustainability. That requires knowledgeable, dedicated people who have the time to help build a future. The challenge is that we need funding to attract those people, but we need those people and their expertise to secure the funding.

Centaur Stride is finally getting closer to that goal, thanks to the people who care enough to help. But we cannot afford to pay the leadership needed to get us there, and without that leadership, securing the resources to sustain the organization becomes even more difficult.

A local financial institution serving more than 9,000 members is the new season sponsor for SUNY Fredonia's Rockefeller Arts Center.

Greater Chautauqua Federal Credit Union (GCFCU) has partnered with Rockefeller to underwrite the 2026-27 performing arts season at Fredonia, which includes the DFT Communications Pops Series, the Walter Gloor Mainstage Series, the Hillman Opera, the Western New York Chamber Orchestra Classics Series and a number of special events.

"We are delighted to welcome Greater Chautauqua Federal Credit Union our season sponsor," said Alison Barry, director Rockefeller Arts Center. "Their support represents an investment not only in the arts, but in the students, families and community members who come together at Rockefeller Arts Center throughout the year. We are grateful for their commitment and look forward to building a strong partnership."

Chief Executive Officer Kelly Haaksma said Greater Chautauqua Federal Credit Union is excited about this partnership with SUNY Fredonia.

"Greater Chautauqua Federal Credit Union is proud to support Rockefeller Arts Center and the important role the arts play in our community," Haaksma said. "This partnership gives us an opportunity to support programming that brings people together, enriches our region, and creates memorable experiences for students and community members alike."

With a focus on serving Chautauqua County residents and building long-term financial relationships, Greater Chautauqua Federal Credit Union supports community-oriented programs, youth savings initiatives, local sponsorships and financial education.

GCFCU operates offices in Falconer, Dunkirk, Jamestown and Mayville. The credit union serves approximately 9,500 members, has roughly $100 million in assets, and employs about 30 staff members.

Established in 1940, the member-owned financial cooperative is headquartered in Falconer and offers a range of consumer and business financial services, including checking and savings accounts, loans, certificates of deposit, online banking, mobile deposit and debit card services.

local.title: Fraternity pitches in at Greystone
local.summary: On a bright Saturday afternoon, members of the Delta Chi fraternity at SUNY Fredonia spent time giving back to the community by volunteering at Greystone Nature Preserve. During a roadside cleanup, one fraternity brother made an unusual discovery: the body of a beautiful bird lying just off the main
local.body:
On a bright Saturday afternoon, members of the Delta Chi fraternity at SUNY Fredonia spent time giving back to the community by volunteering at Greystone Nature Preserve.

During a roadside cleanup, one fraternity brother made an unusual discovery: the body of a beautiful bird lying just off the main road. The brothers named the bird "Mr. Tweetums" and brought it back to the nature preserve, where they held a mock funeral service in its honor. The bird was respectfully laid to rest beneath a beautiful white oak tree.

The brothers' gesture of respect and compassion for the deceased animal was a touching moment and perhaps an unexpected one for those who might not associate fraternity members with such a thoughtful tribute.

The visit to Greystone was an enjoyable experience for the brothers, who regularly participate in community service projects at the preserve. Bill Moran and Diane Clark welcomed the group by sharing their stories and experiences, teaching them about proper land preservation and providing fruit and snacks.

The afternoon also offered opportunities to share traditions and cultural experiences. Clark told the story of Persephone and the pomegranate, prompting one of the brothers, Ninyo, to share a Jewish tradition of eating pomegranates at the beginning of the new year as a symbol of the sweetness hoped for in the year ahead.

The fraternity members also enjoy helping Moran with various maintenance projects around the property. Their work includes turning over the raised garden beds to renew the soil and help preserve the beds for future use.

For the brothers of Delta Chi, volunteering at Greystone Nature Preserve is about more than completing a community service assignment. It provides genuine satisfaction in helping maintain an important piece of natural land while learning the value of conservation and hard work.

Although the projects can be physically demanding, the brothers have been reminded time and again that good things come to those willing to put in the effort.

local.title: Explosive water events blow up plan for district
local.summary: Fredonia’s recent conservation and boil water orders coupled with the explosive water main break on Johnson and Gardner streets highlight several very important facts critical for Fredonia water customers moving forward. First and foremost, the village’s infrastructure will need to be replaced no ma
local.body:
Fredonia's recent conservation and boil water orders coupled with the explosive water main break on Johnson and Gardner streets highlight several very important facts critical for Fredonia water customers moving forward. First and foremost, the village's infrastructure will need to be replaced no matter where the village draws their water from. Regardless of whether the village joins the North County Water District or continues to use their own gravity-fed system, ancient water mains will continue to burst and will continue to deliver discolored water to customers until the mains are replaced. And if the village is buying water from the NCWD, when those ancient water mains burst, as they will until they are replaced, Fredonia will pay for every drop of water lost. Why buy water from Dunkirk or the NCWD only to deliver it through old and corroded pipes and possibly lose large volumes of it by way of water main breaks?

The village's current $22 million plan to join the NCWD does not include the replacement of aging infrastructure. At a village board workshop a few months ago, the idea of adding an infrastructure replacement piece to the NCWD project was discussed. It was stated at the time that replacing some of the more decrepit water mains in the village would cost around $6 million. This idea bubble seemed to burst when the discussion turned to financing both the joining of the NCWD and the replacement of aged infrastructure. At the time it was stated by several key members of village government that the village could not afford to do both. With the NCWD project now paused due to a lack of funds, it would appear that the village cannot afford to join the NCWD anyway.

In October 2025, the village of Fredonia was placed under a water conservation order. Drought conditions had lowered Fredonia's reservoir to a concerning level. There were worries at the time that the village's reservoir would run dry and Fredonians would be left without water. The village has a pump station connected to the city of Dunkirk's water delivery system. This pump station was constructed so that the city and village could provide water to one another during water shortages and emergencies. But in October 2025 inquiring minds were told that the Vineyard Drive pump station couldn't be used as intended due to differences in water system pressure. There were also concerns about water compatibility. Fredonia adds the ion orthophosphate to their water in order to line ancient pipes and prevent metals from leaching into drinking water. In a decision that was widely criticized, the Vineyard Drive pump station was not used in the fall of 2025.

local.body:
The Fredonia Shakespeare Club met at the home of Ms. Susan Westling last week. Following a business meeting, the club heard Ms. Lucille Richardson's presentation on Amy Beach.

Amy Beach (1867 - 1944), formally known during her lifetime as Mrs. H.H.A. Beach, was America's first distinguished and celebrated woman composer of high art music. Overcoming Victorian conventions that largely restricted women to writing amateur parlor songs and teaching pieces, she became one of the first American composers of either gender to achieve international stature. Over her lifetime, she produced a prolific catalog of roughly 300 works. In addition to scores of songs, choral works and solo piano pieces, Beach composed numerous large-scale works. These included a mass, a symphony (the first composed and published by an American woman), a piano concerto, a violin sonata, a piano quintet, a trio, and a one-act opera.

Prodigiously gifted, her talent strikingly apparent almost from infancy, Beach began composing at age four and made her first public appearance as a pianist at age seven. At eighteen, she made her debut with the Boston Symphony Orchestra. That same year, she married a prominent Boston surgeon and yielded to his wish that she limit her public concertizing to focus on composition. Because she was denied formal composition instruction, Beach was self-taught as a composer by studying the works of European masters.

Following her husband's death in 1910, Beach traveled to Europe and achieved enormous success, performing her own works in major cultural centers. Upon returning to the United States just prior to World War I, she was greeted by enthusiastic public acclaim. A major milestone in her career was her fellowship appointment to the renowned MacDowell summer artists' colony in New Hampshire in 1921. Her twenty-year association with the latter inspired a shift in her compositional style, blending her signature lyricism with elements of impressionism and expressionism.

Beach lived and worked extensively in New York City during the final decades of her life. She became closely affiliated with St. Bartholomew's Episcopal Church where her choral compositions were frequently performed, making her a virtual composer-in-residence. Her works continued to be featured in other venues including the MET Orchestra Chamber Ensemble at Carnegie Hall.

Beach died in New York City at the age of 77 and is buried alongside her husband at Forest Hills Cemetery in Boston. Though her music endured a period of neglect after her death, it has experienced a major revival on the concert stage with about two-thirds of her total of 300 works now having been recorded.

local.title: Ground stop lifted, but frustration lingers for travelers at Buffalo airport
local.summary: On Friday, an earlier nationwide ground stop threw travel plans into chaos, leaving passengers waiting for answers as delays and cancellations disrupted flights.
local.body: The national ground stop may be over, but it could be some time before the aviation system gets back on track.At Buffalo Niagara International Airport, travelers told 7 News they were frustrated and uncertain about when they would finally be able to reach their destinations.An earlier nationwide ground stop threw travel plans into chaos, leaving passengers waiting for answers as delays and cancellations disrupted flights.For some, the uncertainty was enough to reconsider traveling altogether.Jim Rivera was headed to Atlanta to visit his daughter, but he said he would rather get a refund than risk traveling."Right now, we feel like we shouldn’t be traveling. What is going on in the air and on the ground is not safe to travel at this moment," Rivera said.Other passengers were dealing with missed connections and canceled plans.Ever Miranda said her flight to Fort Lauderdale was canceled. She was traveling for work and worried the disruption could cause her to miss her little sister’s birthday."I might miss my little sister’s birthday," Miranda said.Even after the ground stop was lifted, travelers were still waiting for updates and trying to figure out when they would get home.David Brown said he was growing frustrated with the uncertainty and did not even want to leave his spot in the airport because he feared getting stuck somewhere else."I am just going crazy here. I need to eat, and I don’t want to go inside yet because I don’t want to be stuck in one place," Brown said.Some travelers decided they did not want to wait any longer, turning to rental cars for another way home. For some, that meant facing more than 20 hours on the road.Adam Vanbrekel said driving offered more certainty than waiting for another flight.“I want to get back home, and then I know I’ll guarantee I make it there rather than guessing,” Vanbrekel said.Dylan Wood and his group also decided to drive rather than wait without knowing when they would be able to depart.“We didn't want to just sit and wait and not really have an answer on when we can actually depart, so just a group decision that we just decided to drive,” Wood said.WATCH: Ground stop lifted, but frustration lingers for travelers at Buffalo airportWhether waiting for a flight or hitting the road, travelers shared one common goal: getting home safely.While flights are beginning to resume, delays and cancellations may continue. local.title: NIAGARA DISCOVERIES: Madison McCollum, Civil War vet and Porter dairy farmer
local.summary: This past Wednesday, Veterans Day was observed across the United States with parades, ceremonies, wreath-layings and the distribution of poppies, the symbol of remembrance. Over the last 200+ years, tens of thousands of men from Niagara County have served in…
local.body:
This past Wednesday, Veterans Day was observed across the United States with parades, ceremonies, wreath-layings and the distribution of poppies, the symbol of remembrance. Over the last 200+ years, tens of thousands of men from Niagara County have served in the armed forces and thousands have been killed in action. Many of those servicemen are well-known, while others have been lost to history. Here is the story of two of brother soldiers, one came home and one who didn’t.

The surname “McCollum” is very well-known in the history of Niagara County. Joel McCollum was one of the earliest settlers in what is now the city of Lockport and McCollum descendants still reside in the family homestead at North Adams and Vine streets. There was another McCollum family in the town of Porter, prosperous farmers and well-respected citizens, some of whom served with distinction in the Civil War.

Ann Marie Linnabery is the assistant director of the History Center of Niagara.

local.summary: Mark Jacobs has lived a fair share of his life in other countries, working in U.S. embassies on three continents and speaking languages such as Spanish, Turkish, and the Guarani used in parts of Paraguay.
local.body:
Former Niagara Fall resident Mark Jacobs has published seven books.

Mark Jacobs has lived a fair share of his life in other countries, working in U.S. embassies on three continents and speaking languages such as Spanish, Turkish, and the Guarani used in parts of Paraguay.

But the Niagara Falls native still remembers his hometown well, using it among various other exotic locales in his novels and short stories. His newest book, “Memory Falls,” which will be released in January through Regal House Publishing, delves into a local community not many outside of Western New York are familiar with.

At a time when Republicans suffered significant setbacks across the country, the Republican Majority of the Niagara County Legislature bucked the national trend with a tremendous victory. The results demonstrate that when local government stays focused on the issues that matter to residents, voters recognize the difference.

Tuesday’s election sent a clear message about the direction of Niagara County, and it was a message worth paying attention to. At a time when Republicans suffered significant setbacks across the country, the Republican Majority of the Niagara County Legislature bucked the national trend with a tremendous victory. The results demonstrate that when local government stays focused on the issues that matter to residents, voters recognize the difference.

This victory did not happen by accident. It is the result of a governing philosophy built around pragmatic problem solving, fiscal responsibility and standing up for Niagara County when outside interests threaten our communities.

entertainment.title: Can You Feel It in the Air Tonight? 11 Best Moments From 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony
entertainment.summary: From Cynthia Erivo & Travis Barker doing *the* drum break justice to the Red Hot Chilli Peppers donning Rick Rubin wigs, these were our highlights.
entertainment.body:
While many of the headlines leading up to the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony this weekend were about who wouldn’t be there, our highlights from Saturday night’s (Nov. 14) show at L.A.’s Peacock Theatre are all about who showed up and showed out.

The night was bookended by two surprise performances, starting with 2005 inductees U2 playing a brand-new song and a classic to kick things off and ending with 2001 inductees Aerosmith joining forces with 2009 inductees Run-DMC to perform their pioneering rock/hip-hop mash-up “Walk This Way,” a top five Billboard Hot 100 smash in 1986.

In between, a mixture of rising stars and bona fide legends showed up to either introduce or pay musical tribute to the Class of 2026 — or, in some cases, the inductees themselves got in on the action. The full Wu-Tang Clan hit the stage for a medley, while Queen Latifah and MC Lyte joined forces for a joint performance celebrating their contributions as women in hip-hop, Billy Idol and his longtime guitarist Steve Stevens did one solo song and one duet with a famous face, and Peter Hook of Joy Division and New Order was surrounded by superfans for a celebration of his dual groups.

The through-line of the night was innovation. While the Rock Hall has expanded far beyond the genre of rock & roll, each member of the new class has something vital in common: They changed music for generations to come.

Below, find Billboard ‘s best moments from the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony, which will air Dec. 8 from 8-11 p.m. ET on ABC and stream on Disney+ the next day.

U2 crashed the Rock Hall ceremony, opening the show with a surprise two-song set a day after releasing their new album, Carnaval De Luz . The band wasn’t on the bill — they were inducted back in 2005, their first year of eligibility — but they kicked off the night with “Silencio,” the album’s second single, joined by a line of performers dressed as riot police and carrying shields, then closed with 1984’s “Pride (In the Name of Love).” The twofer from the Hall of Fame vets set the tone for an evening of legends only.
